message.content:
Below is a “cook‑book” style walk‑through that shows you **three** practical ways to grab a screenshot of whatever page is currently displayed in Google Chrome – all from a Python script. | Goal | What you’ll need | Why it works | |------|------------------|--------------| | **1️⃣ Grab the page that’s already open in your *running* Chrome** | 1. Start Chrome with the `--remote-debugging-port` flag.
2. Use a DevTools‑Protocol wrapper (`pychrome`, `pyppeteer`, or `playwright`). | Chrome exposes a JSON‑over‑HTTP API when you enable remote debugging. The wrappers let you talk to that API and ask Chrome to capture a screenshot. | | **2️⃣ Open a fresh headless Chrome instance and screenshot a URL** | Selenium + ChromeDriver (or Playwright). | Selenium drives a new browser process; you can tell it to go to a URL and then call `save_screenshot`. | | **3️⃣ Take a screenshot of the *visible* part of the Chrome window (no DevTools)** | `pyautogui` (or Pillow + `mss`). | These libraries capture the screen (or a region) like a normal screenshot tool. | --- ## 1️⃣ Screenshot the *currently open* tab in an existing Chrome window ### Step 1 – Launch Chrome with remote debugging ```bash # macOS / Linux /Applications/Google\ Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google\ Chrome \ --remote-debugging-port=9222 \ --user-data-dir=/tmp/chrome_debug_profile # Windows "C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe" ^ --remote-debugging-port=9222 ^ --user-data-dir=%TEMP%\chrome_debug_profile ``` > **Why?** > The `--remote-debugging-port` flag tells Chrome to expose its DevTools Protocol on that port. > The `--user-data-dir` flag creates a fresh profile so you don’t interfere with your normal browsing session. > **Tip:** If you’re already running Chrome, you can open a new window with the flag by launching a *second* instance (the first one stays untouched). ### Step 2 – Install a DevTools wrapper ```bash pip install pychrome # or: pip install pyppeteer # or: pip install playwright ``` ### Option A – Using **pychrome** ```python import base64 import pychrome # Connect to the running Chrome instance browser = pychrome.Browser(url="http://127.0.0.1:9222") # Find the *active* tab (the one you’re looking at) tabs = browser.list_tab() active_tab = next((t for t in tabs if t.active), None) if not active_tab: raise RuntimeError("No active tab found") # Tell Chrome to capture a screenshot of the current page active_tab.start() screenshot_data = active_tab.call_method("Page.captureScreenshot")["data"] # Decode the base64 PNG and write it to disk with open("screenshot.png", "wb") as f: f.write(base64.b64decode(screenshot_data)) print("Screenshot saved to screenshot.png") ``` > **What happens?** > `Page.captureScreenshot` returns a base64‑encoded PNG. We decode it and write it to a file. ### Option B – Using **pyppeteer** (connect to an existing instance) ```python import asyncio import base64 from pyppeteer import connect async def main(): # Connect to the existing Chrome instance browser = await connect(browserURL="http://127.0.0.1:9222") # Grab the first page (the active tab) pages = await browser.pages() page = pages[0] # Usually the active tab is first # Capture screenshot (returns bytes) screenshot_bytes = await page.screenshot() # Write to disk with open("screenshot.png", "wb") as f: f.write(screenshot_bytes) await browser.disconnect() asyncio.get_event_loop().run_until_complete(main()) ``` > **Why pyppeteer?** > It’s a Python port of Puppeteer (Node.js). It gives you a higher‑level API than raw CDP calls. ### Option C – Using **Playwright** (connect over CDP) ```python from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright with sync_playwright() as p: # Connect to the running Chrome instance browser = p.chromium.connect_over_cdp("http://127.0.0.1:9222") # Grab the first context & page context = browser.contexts[0] page = context.pages[0] # Capture screenshot page.screenshot(path="screenshot.png") browser.disconnect() ``` > **Why Playwright?** > It supports multiple browsers (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit) and has a very clean sync/async API. --- ## 2️⃣ Screenshot a URL in a *new* headless Chrome instance (Selenium) ```python from selenium import webdriver from selenium.webdriver.chrome.service import Service from selenium.webdriver.chrome.options import Options from webdriver_manager.chrome import ChromeDriverManager options = Options() options.add_argument("--headless") # Run without UI options.add_argument("--disable-gpu") # Needed on Windows options.add_argument("--window-size=1920,1080") # Full HD driver = webdriver.Chrome(service=Service(ChromeDriverManager().install()), options=options) driver.get("https://www.example.com") driver.save_screenshot("screenshot.png") driver.quit() ``` > **Why Selenium?** > It’s the de‑facto standard for browser automation. The `save_screenshot` method writes a PNG of the viewport. --- ## 3️⃣ Screenshot the *visible* part of the Chrome window (no DevTools) If you just want a “normal” screenshot of what you see on the screen (including the Chrome UI), you can use `pyautogui`: ```python import pyautogui # Grab the entire screen pyautogui.screenshot("full_screen.png") # Or grab a region (x, y, width, height) region = (100, 200, 800, 600) # Example coordinates pyautogui.screenshot("region.png", region=region) ``` > **Caveat:** > This captures whatever is on the screen, not just the webpage. If you need a clean, full‑page screenshot, use one of the CDP methods above. --- ## Quick Checklist | ✅ | Item | |----|------| | ✅ | Start Chrome with `--remote-debugging-port=9222` | | ✅ | Install a CDP wrapper (`pychrome`, `pyppeteer`, or `playwright`) | | ✅ | Connect to the running instance (`Browser(url="http://127.0.0.1:9222")`) | | ✅ | Grab the active tab (`list_tab()` → filter by `active`) | | ✅ | Call `Page.captureScreenshot` (or the wrapper’s equivalent) | | ✅ | Decode base64 PNG and write to disk | --- ### TL;DR Code (pychrome) ```python import base64, pychrome browser = pychrome.Browser(url="http://127.0.0.1:9222") tab = next(t for t in browser.list_tab() if t.active) tab.start() png_base64 = tab.call_method("Page.captureScreenshot")["data"] with open("screenshot.png", "wb") as f: f.write(base64.b64decode(png_base64)) ``` Run Chrome with `--remote-debugging-port=9222` first, then execute the script. You’ll get a PNG of whatever page you’re looking at. Happy screenshotting!
